activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Benjamin had a red shirt with a big number three. It was his team shirt for soccer. He wanted to kick the ball into the net. But the ball was still. It sat on the grass like a rock.

A butterfly landed on the grass near him. Benjamin watched it open and close its wings. Then he ran to see it better. The butterfly flew up. It flew away over the fence. Benjamin kept watching it.

Then he saw something. The wind was blowing. The wind pushed the butterfly up and away. The wind also pushed a leaf across the grass. Benjamin looked at the ball. The wind pushed the ball too. It rolled a little bit toward the net. Benjamin ran and kicked it. The ball went in. "Goal!" said Daddy from the side. Benjamin jumped up and down and hugged his juicy orange slice after the game.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Wyatt sat at the little table in art class. He wanted to paint his cat, Max. But his cat looked like a big blob on the paper. Wyatt felt upset. "My cat looks like a puddle," he said.

Miss Amy sat down next to him. "Let's look at Max in the picture," she said. Wyatt looked. Max had a round head. A circle! His ears were pointy triangles. His body was long like a rectangle. His food bowl was a square.

Wyatt painted a circle first. Then he painted two triangles on top. Then a long rectangle for the body. A square for the bowl.

"It's Max!" said Wyatt. "I made a cat from shapes!" He painted a tiny green plant in the corner too. Then he held his picture up high for everyone to see.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Hazel loved the little kitchen at school. She wanted to play house with her friend Mia. But Mia was already holding the baby doll.

"You be the big sister," said Mia. "I am the mama."

Hazel did not want to be the big sister. She wanted to be the mama too. Her lip went wobbly. She almost wanted to yell.

Then Hazel saw the tiny teddy bear on the shelf. It sat all alone in the middle of the rug. Nobody was holding it.

"Your baby is crying," Hazel said. She picked up the teddy. She patted its back, nice and slow. She gave it a soft hug.

Mia watched. "The teddy needs a mama," said Mia.

"Yes," said Hazel. "I will be its mama."

Hazel wrapped the teddy in a small blanket. She fed it a pretend bottle. The teddy stopped crying.

Mia brought a little cup. "Tea for two mamas?" she asked.

"Yes, please," said Hazel.

They sat together by the toy kitchen. Two mamas, two babies, one happy tea party.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came on the big bus. He carried one red bag. Ali wanted Grandpa to stay in his room, but the crib was too small.

"I am too big for that bed," said Grandpa. Ali felt sad. Then he saw the big bed in the guest room. Mom let Grandpa put his bag there. Grandpa would sleep in the big bed for a whole week.

Ali wanted to make Grandpa's bed cozy. He put his teddy bear on the pillow. Then he put a banana next to the bear. Mom laughed. "That will not be comfy," she said.

Ali took the banana away. He put a soft blanket on instead. Grandpa patted the bed. "Soft as a cloud," he said. He lay down and hugged the teddy bear. The bear's hat fell over Grandpa's nose.

"That hat tickles," said Grandpa. Ali giggled and giggled. Grandpa put the hat on Ali's head instead. It was much too big. "A tidy bed and a silly hat," said Grandpa. "Best room in the house."

Ali carried a pillow to the floor. He lay down next to the bed. "I sleep here too," he said. Grandpa snored a small pretend snore. Ali snored back.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Clara rode in the car to the big field. Her team wore red shirts. The grass smelled green and fresh. The dirt was soft under her shoes.

Clara wanted to hit the ball far. She held the bat with both hands. Coach tossed the ball. Clara swung. Miss. She waited and tried again. Swing. Miss again. The bat felt heavy, so she held it tighter.

Coach tossed a slow one. Clara swung hard. Tink! The ball hit the bat and flew over the dirt. It rolled and rolled into the quiet green grass. Clara dropped the bat and ran. Her feet went fast, fast, fast. The crowd made a big happy sound.

Her friend Ben picked up the ball and threw it back. "Good hit, Clara!" said Coach. Clara patted the bat gently. "You did that," she whispered to it. Then she ran to her place in the field, and the sun felt warm on her red shirt.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Luka went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about big trucks. The library was quiet. Too quiet. Luka felt a little scared of the tall shelves.

A girl sat at a small table. She cried soft tears. Her book had a torn page. She looked sad. Luka found a sticky dot on the table. He pressed it over the tear. The page lay flat again. The girl smiled a big smile. Now she looked happy.

Luka asked the librarian, "Where are truck books?" The librarian pointed. Luka ran. Then he stopped. Running made the librarian frown. Luka said sorry. He walked like a cat instead. He found a truck book with a shiny red cover. His eyes went wide. He felt so excited. At home, he read it three times with mom. "A sweet end to a good day," mom said. Luka hugged the book.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
It was a stormy summer day, so Sienna went to the community centre. Miss Ana put crackers on two plates.

"Which plate has more?" asked Miss Ana.

Sienna pointed at the big plate. "That one!" But Ben said, "No, my plate has more!"

Sienna counted the big plate. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted Ben's plate. "One, two, three, four." Ben had fewer crackers. "Five is more than four," said Sienna.

Ben looked sad, like he might cry. "Count again," he said. "Start with the round cracker."

Sienna counted from the round one. "One, two, three, four, five. Still five!"

Then Ben counted his own plate backwards. "Four, three, two, one. Still four!"

Miss Ana gave Ben one more cracker. Ben grinned and counted fast. "One, two, three, four, five. Five!"

"Now we both have five," said Sienna. "Hooray!"

They munched their crackers together.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Parker stood by the little pool in the backyard. His dad was in the water, holding out his arms. "Come in, Parker," said Dad. Parker wanted to swim to Dad, but his feet would not move.

Then Parker saw a green ball float by the edge. He reached out and pushed it. The ball went splash, and it slid across the water. Parker looked at his hands. He pushed the water the same way. His body moved forward, right into Dad's arms.

"I swam!" said Parker. "You did," said Dad. Parker pushed the water again and again. He chased the green ball all the way to the other side. "Lunch soon," said Dad. Parker laughed and splashed one more time. "Again," he said, reaching for the ball.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Emily wanted warm soup for lunch. Mom put a big pot on the stove. Emily stood far away and watched. The pot was big. Her little cup was small. "Mom, will the soup get hot?" she asked. "Yes, very hot," said Mom.

Emily put a small jug of milk on the table. The milk was cold. She touched the jug with one finger. Brrr. Then Mom poured the soup into a bowl. The bowl sat and sat. Emily waited. Was it still too hot? Mom helped her blow on it. The steam went away. Now Emily touched the bowl. It was warm, not hot. "It changed!" said Emily.

Emily ate fast, and the soup went down to the bottom. She ate slow, and the bowl stayed full. Then she saw something in her cup. A noodle had fallen in the milk. It floated and wiggled. It looked like it could swim. Emily laughed. "Mom, look! My noodle is swimming in the cold milk." Mom came to look, and the noodle bobbed up and down, small and white in the big blue cup.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Milo went to the farmers' market with Dad. He saw big red tomatoes on a table. He wanted to grow his own tomatoes at home.

Dad bought a small tomato plant in a pot. Milo held the pot near his tummy all the way home. In the yard, Dad dug a hole. Milo set the plant in the hole. Dad pushed the dirt back. Then Milo watered the dirt with his little can.

Days went by. The plant stood tall. Small yellow flowers came out. Then Milo saw a tiny green ball near a flower. "Dad, look!" said Milo. Dad smiled. The flower had made a little tomato. Milo watered the plant every day. The green ball grew big and red. Dad picked it with two hands. "My tomato," said Milo. He held it up to the warm sun.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Hunter ran out to the school playground. His little blue truck was gone. "Where did you go?" he asked. He looked under the slide. He looked by the swing. No truck.

Then Hunter saw the wind blow a red leaf. The leaf rolled across the ground. It stopped by the fence. Hunter stopped too. "Did the wind move my truck?" he said out loud. "Maybe it did. I will look where the wind goes."

He walked to the fence. The wind had pushed papers there too. One paper was his friend Mia's. "Is this yours?" he asked. "Yes! Thank you, that was polite," said Mia. They looked together by the fence.

Mia pointed. "Look, Hunter. Something blue." It was the truck, tucked in the grass. Hunter held it to his heart. "Now we can play," he said. "You can pretend it is a race car," said Mia. Hunter pushed the truck, and the wheels went round and round, all the way to the sandbox.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Daniel sat in his car seat. He looked for his doll. Where was it? "I had it yesterday," he said. Yesterday was the day at Grandma's house. The doll was lost.

Dad said, "We are going to Grandma's house now." Daniel looked out the window. He saw one tree. Then two trees. Then three trees. "Are we there now?" he asked. "Not now," said Dad. "Later." So Daniel watched. One cow. Two cows. Three cows. Then Dad pulled the car over. They were there! Grandma held the doll in her hand. She had found it under her big chair. "You left it here yesterday," she said. Daniel hugged his doll tight. "Today we drive home," he said. "Tomorrow I will show Bear the doll." He climbed back in his seat. "Now we can go," said Daniel. Dad smiled and buckled him in.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Felix sat at the kitchen table. His apple waited on his plate. But his hands were messy from playing in the sand. He looked at his fingers. They were dusty and a little stinky.

"I want my apple now," said Felix.

Mom said, "First we wash. Then we eat."

Felix went to the sink. Mom turned on the water. It was warm and gentle. She put soap on his hands. "Now we make bubbles," she said. "We sing the happy song two times."

Felix rubbed his hands together. Bubbles grew big and white. He sang the song once. He kept rubbing. He sang it again. "Are twenty seconds done yet?" he asked.

"Yes, all done," said Mom.

She helped him rinse. The bubbles slid down the drain. The water carried the dust away too. Felix held up his hands. They were clean and shiny. "Where did the dirt go?" he asked.

"Down the drain," said Mom. "The water took it."

"I made bubbles, and the bubbles took the dirt!" said Felix.

"Sing it again," said Mom with a smile.

"Bubbles took the dirt! Bubbles took the dirt!"

Then Felix dried his hands on the little towel. He sat down and picked up his apple. He took one big, happy bite. His clean hands held it tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Chloe was cold. She wanted to go outside and play. She pulled her coat off the hook. The coat had a big zipper. Chloe pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. The coat hung crooked. One sleeve was inside out, like a hiding place for her hand.

Mama waited by the door. She did not hurry. Chloe pulled the sleeve out. She shook her arm. The sleeve popped out, all warm. Chloe laid the coat on the wood floor. She pushed her arms in again. This time the coat sat just right.

The zipper was stuck at the bottom. Chloe pulled it up, down, up. The zipper slid, and the coat closed all the way to her chin. Chloe patted the zipper. "I did it," she said. Mama smiled and opened the door. Cold air rushed in. Chloe ran out to the wild, windy yard.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Alexis lived with Grandma for a whole rainy week. On Monday he lost his favorite red sock. "It went somewhere," said Grandma. "Let's look."

They looked under the bed. Alexis found one dusty shoe. They looked behind the chair. He found two paper balls. "Not socks," said Alexis.

They counted what they found, out loud. One, two, three hair pins in a jar. Four, five, six shiny buttons in a cup. "My sock is not here," said Alexis. His lip went down.

Grandma hummed a counting song. "Seven, eight, nine," she sang, peeking into the warm laundry basket. It smelled like soap and clean towels.

Alexis lifted a folded towel. There it was, sock number ten. "You were hiding!" he said. He hugged the soft, warm sock to his cheek.

Grandma laughed. "Ten things found, one happy boy," she said, and she poured warm milk for them both.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Abigail could not find her bunny. She looked under her pillow. No bunny there. She looked in her toy box. No bunny there either.

"Bunny is lost," said Abigail. "I want my real bunny back."

Dad came to help. "Let's look in your room," he said. First they picked up the blocks. Then Dad helped Abigail clean the floor. They put the blocks in the box.

Abigail pulled the blanket off the bed. She pulled it all the way down. Then something happened. Bunny slid off the bed with the blanket. Bunny slid right onto the clean floor.

"Bunny!" said Abigail. She gave Bunny a big hug. Bunny was dusty from under the blanket.

Abigail brushed Bunny off with her hand. "You slid down," she told Bunny. "I found you."

Dad smiled. "Blankets make things slide," he said. "Now let's tuck Bunny in tight."

Abigail laid Bunny on the pillow. She pulled the blanket up, just a little bit. Bunny stayed safe and warm.

"Good night, Bunny," said Abigail.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Ellie went to the pet store with Dad. She wanted a fish of her own. "Can I pick one?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. Ellie looked at all the fish. One little fish was orange. It swam right up to her hand on the glass. "That one," said Ellie.

At home, Dad helped her set up the bowl. Ellie put in the water and the little stones. The fish swam around and around. Then it bumped the glass, and bumped it again. "Is it sorry?" Ellie asked. "I think it wants food," said Dad. He showed Ellie the tiny food jar. Ellie turned the lid and dropped one small bit in. The fish saw the food. It swam fast and gobbled it up. Ellie clapped her hands. "You were hungry!" she said. The fish blew a little bubble. Ellie dropped in one more bit, and the fish chased it all around the bowl.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Leon was in the backyard. He had two cups of paint. One cup was red. One cup was yellow.

"I want green," said Leon. He looked and looked. There was no green paint.

Mama sat with him on the grass. "Let's mix," she said. Leon put his brush in the red cup. Drip, drip. Then he put it in the yellow cup. Swish, swish.

Red and yellow made orange! The paint was orange like a pumpkin. Leon touched it with one finger. It was cool and smooth.

"Now I need blue," said Leon. Mama brought a cup of blue paint. Blue like the ocean, deep and dark. Leon mixed blue and yellow. Swish, swish, swish.

Green! Green like the grass! Leon laughed. He painted a big green leaf.

Then his cup tipped over. The red paint sank into the grass. "Sorry, grass," said Leon softly. Mama wiped his hands with a warm cloth.

"I can make orange, and green, and..." Leon held up his brush. "What can red and blue make?"

Mama smiled. "Let's see."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Connor and his mom walked into the hotel room. Connor carried his little brown bear. "This is our room for tonight," said Mom. Connor looked around. There was a big bed and a big window.

Soon it was nap time. Connor lay down with his bear. But the sun came in through the window. It was too bright. Connor put his hands over his eyes. "I can't sleep," he said. Mom said, "Maybe you can fix that."

Connor looked at the window. There were big curtains. He pulled them across, all by himself. The curtains covered the window. The room went dark and cozy. The sun could not come in anymore.

"Mom, look!" Connor yelled. "I made it dark!" Mom smiled. "Good job, kid," she said. She tucked him in. Connor hugged his bear tight. Then Mom gave him a kiss on his head. The dark room felt soft and warm. Soon all Mom could hear was a small snore from the bed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Aiden sat on Grandpa's lap. The big game was on TV. "Red team, blue team," Aiden said. "Red team, blue team." Grandma laughed and clapped.

Grandpa had a little pot of face paint. "Hold still," he said. He painted a small red star on Aiden's cheek. Aiden looked in the mirror. The star was red and shiny. He pointed one finger at it. "Star!" he said.

The whistle blew. It was a sharp sound. Everyone jumped up. "Go, go, go!" they shouted. Grandpa waved his arms. Aunt Mei stomped her feet. Aiden clapped his hands too. Then the baby cousin woke up. She cried and cried. The room got very quiet.

Aiden slid off the lap. He found the baby's soft blanket. He gave it to her, very gently. The baby stopped crying. She grabbed one of his fingers and held on tight. On the TV, the crowd cheered again, but this time the family clapped softly, quiet as mice. The baby smiled at Aiden. "More game," Aiden whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Hayden went to the pharmacy with his mom. He wanted a snack from his bag. He sat on the bench next to the sink. His hands felt sticky and sandy.

Mom turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. Hayden put his hands under it. The water ran like rain over his fingers. Mom gave him one pump of soap. The bubbles were white and small. They counted together. One, two, three, four, five. The bubbles turned gray. Six, seven, eight, nine, ten. The gray ran down the drain. Eleven, twelve, all the way to twenty. Now the bubbles were white and clean.

Hayden rinsed off the soap. He looked at his hands in the mirror. His shadow waved back at him. He held his hands up. "Clean!" he said. Mom opened his snack bag. Hayden ate his crackers, one by one. Then he wiped his hands on the towel. "Twenty next time too," he said, and jumped off the bench.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Eva sat on the red rug at school. Miss Jo held up her hands. "Today we will sing a song," she said. Eva wanted to sing the whole song by herself. But she did not know it yet.

Miss Jo clapped her hands. clap, clap, clap. Eva watched. When Miss Jo clapped, her hands made a sound. When she stopped, the room was quiet. Eva tried to clap too. Her hands went fast, fast, fast. "Too fast," said Miss Jo with a smile. "Try to help me. Watch my hands first." So Eva watched. She waited. Then she clapped when Miss Jo clapped. clap, clap, clap. Now the sounds went together.

Then Miss Jo sang the rhyme. "Hickory dickory dock." She sang it two times. Eva listened with her big ears. She asked herself, "Can I remember the words?" She took a big breath and tried. "Hickory dickory dock, the mouse ran up the clock." The words came out. All of them! The class clapped for her, one clap, then a huge round of claps. Eva stood up tall and sang it one more time. "The clock struck one," she sang, "the mouse ran down. Hickory dickory dock."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Weston ran into Grandma's kitchen. He saw a big bowl of white snow. "Is it cold?" he asked. Grandma laughed. "It is ice cream. You can help."

Weston sat on his tall stool. He wanted to make his favorite color, blue. Grandma gave him little bottles. Each bottle had a color inside. "One drop," said Grandma.

Weston squeezed one drop of blue. The white snow turned blue like the sky! He clapped his hands. Then he dropped yellow. Green spread out like grass! "How?" said Weston. He made a puzzle face.

Grandma held up a spoon. "Try red and yellow," she said. Weston tried. The ice cream turned orange like a pumpkin. He dropped red and blue too. Purple swirled around and around.

Grandma scooped it into a bowl. Weston took one little bite. "It tastes like berries and sun!" he said. Grandma smiled and gave him a red spoon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Jackson ran to the park with his red ball. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Jackson wore his t-shirt and shorts.

Then the wind began to blow. It was windy now. The wind pushed the last leaf off the big tree. The leaf flew up, up, up. "Come back, leaf!" Jackson called. The wind pushed his ball too. The ball rolled far away.

A girl named Mia chased the ball for him. She wore a jacket because she was cold. Jackson rubbed his arms. "Here," Mia said. "My mom has a spare sweater." Jackson put it on. Then clouds came. Big drops fell. It was rainy now. Mia opened her umbrella. Jackson stood under it with her. They watched the rain color the gray path dark. "Want to share a snack?" Mia asked. Jackson smiled and held out his hand for a cracker.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Wren sat at the big table. She had a pencil and some paper. "I want to write my name," she said.

Mama sat next to her. "Let's try," said Mama. Wren grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The letters came out fat and wobbly. The W looked like a squiggle. The R fell over on its face.

"Why do my letters fall down?" asked Wren.

"Hold the pencil like this," said Mama. She showed Wren how to pinch it with two fingers, nice and light.

Wren pinched the pencil. She touched the paper soft and slow. The W came out pointy. The R stood up tall. "It works!" said Wren.

She wrote W, then R, then E, then N. "Wren!" she said. She wrote it again. Then she wrote it all alone, with no help at all.

Mama taped the paper to the fridge. Wren smiled at her name, standing up straight. "I can write my name," said Wren, "all by myself."

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Jasmine skipped into the school cafeteria. It was her first day of school. She held her lunch tray with two hands. On the tray was a tasty cheese sandwich and a little juice box.

Jasmine wanted her juice. But the straw was tricky. She pushed the straw down. Then she squeezed the box hard. Squirt! Juice went right up her nose. A boy named Ben laughed. "Do juice boxes bite?" Jasmine asked. "No," said Ben. "They just squirt if you squeeze them."

Jasmine tried again. She held the box soft and gentle. She took a little sip. No squirt! The juice was sweet and cold. From the kitchen door, a cook waved a big spoon at her. Jasmine held up her juice box and took a proud, tiny sip.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Arthur ran up the steps to Milo's house. He carried his blue teddy bear under one arm. Milo opened the door with a big smile.

"Let's play house!" said Milo. He pointed to a blanket over two chairs. "This is our home. My doll is the baby." But the baby doll had no bed. Milo looked and looked. No box was big enough.

Then Arthur saw something. He put his teddy down in a basket. The basket was round and soft, like a nest. The teddy fit just right! "Can the baby sleep here too?" Arthur asked. Milo nodded fast. "Yes! It is a perfect bed."

The baby doll went into the basket next to the teddy. Milo whispered, "Shh, the baby is sleeping." Arthur whispered too. He tucked the blanket up to the doll's chin.

Milo's mom came in with two cups of warm milk. "How is the baby?" she asked quietly. "Sleeping in her nest!" said Arthur. He picked up a toy spoon and fed the teddy a pretend snack. Milo laughed and clapped.

"Now the baby needs a hat," said Milo. He ran to get a small sock. Arthur held the doll still while Milo pulled it on.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Muhammad sat at the dinner table. His bowl was empty. He wanted more soup, but the big pot was far away.

"Mama, more please," he said. Mama picked up the ladle. She turned the pot slowly. Hot steam rose up, so Muhammad stayed in his chair and watched. Mama filled his bowl. The soup went up, up, up, to the top.

Muhammad ate his soup. Then he ate bread. Then his tummy felt round like a ball. He yawned a big yawn.

Papa said, "Bath time first." Muhammad ran to the bathroom. Papa turned the tap and the tub filled with bubbles. Muhammad splashed and washed his toes.

After the bath, Muhammad put on his soft pajamas. The buttons were small, so he pulled them through one by one. Then he brushed his teeth at the sink.

He went to his room. His lamp was still on. He climbed into bed and pulled the blanket up. Papa turned the lamp off. The room went dark and quiet. Muhammad closed his eyes. "Good night, stars," he whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Maya was four today. Her party was at the park. There was a big table with a cake on it. Grandma had put four candles on top. Dad lit the candles with a match. Maya stood back and watched.

Then the wind blew. The candle flames bent and wobbled. Maya gasped. One flame went out. Then another flame went out. The wind had blown them out. Maya had an idea.

"Can the wind blow out all of them?" she asked.

Grandma smiled. "You can try," she said.

Maya took a big breath. She puffed hard like the wind. The last two flames went out. A little smoke curled up. Everyone clapped and cheered.

"Now we sing," said Mom. The family sang the birthday song. Maya's cup tipped over and juice began to spill. Grandma caught it with a napkin. "No problem," Grandma said.

They ate cake on the grass. Maya said, "The wind puffed, and I puffed, and the candles went out." She took another big bite.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Hazel held her bunny in the store. Then she let go to grab a big red apple. The apple went into the cart. But bunny was gone.

"Where did bunny go?" Hazel asked.

Mama made the cart go slow. They looked down each aisle. They saw bread and milk and jam. No bunny.

Then Hazel stopped. She put her apple on the floor. She gave it a little push. The apple rolled far, under the shelf. The round apple made it all the way to the wall.

"Bunny might roll too," Hazel said.

She got down on her knees. She peeked under the shelf. It was dark in there. She saw a soft gray ear.

Mama reached in with her long arm. Out came bunny, with a bit of dust on his nose.

Hazel gave bunny a hug. Then she put him deep in her pocket, where he could not fall out.

"My apple found you," she whispered.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Athena was playing in the backyard. Her toy train sat on the grass. Grandma was by the grill at the far end.

A butterfly flew by. It was orange. Athena wanted to follow it.

"Stay close to Grandma," said Grandma. Athena counted her steps. One, two, three. The butterfly landed on the fence. Athena wanted to go to the fence.

Grandma held her hand. "The grill is hot," said Grandma. Athena looked at the grill. It was silver and big. It made a sizzling sound. Grandma put a bun near it with a long spoon. Athena saw the spoon. It was not for touching. That was the rule.

The butterfly flew again. It landed on Grandma's shoulder. "Look," said Athena. "It stays close too." Grandma laughed. "That butterfly is neat," she said.

The buns were ready. Grandma put the hot food on a plate. Athena waited on the grass with her train. She pushed the train. Choo, choo. The butterfly sat nearby.

Athena ate her bun at the little table. The bun was warm and good. The butterfly sat on the fence in the sun. Grandma poured cold water into a cup. Athena touched the cup. It felt cool on her hands.

"Stay close, stay safe," said Grandma. Athena snuggled next to her. The train went choo, choo, round and round.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Ellie sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. "Will the shot hurt?" she asked. "Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then we get ice cream." The nurse came in with a little bandage and a small needle. "Look at me," said Mom. "We can count together."

"One, two, three," they counted. Ellie squeezed Mom's hand. The nurse said, "All done." Ellie looked at her arm. The pinch was over already. The nurse pressed a round bandage on it. The bandage was pink with little stars. "You were so smart to sit still," said Mom.

Outside, the clouds began to rain. Ellie and Mom ran to the ice cream shop. Ellie licked a cold, sweet strawberry cone. Rain tapped on the window. Mom wiped Ellie's sticky chin. "My arm is all better," said Ellie. She held up her star bandage for Mom to kiss.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Ayla was at Grandma's house. It was a cloudy day. "Let's play a game," said Grandma. She held up a card with a big letter on it.

"Can you find this letter in the room?" asked Grandma. The card had a big B on it. Ayla looked around. She saw a book on the table. She pointed at it. "B!" she said. Grandma smiled. "And B makes a buh sound," she said. "Buh, buh, book."

Ayla wanted to find more. She looked at the basket by the chair. "Ball!" she said. It started with B too. She touched the ball. It was smooth and bouncy. "Buh, buh, ball," she said all by herself.

Then Grandma held up a card with a big M on it. Hmm. Ayla looked and looked. Where was an M? Then she saw the milk glass on the tray. She ran over and put her little hand on it. The glass was cold. "Mmm, milk!" she said. Grandma clapped her hands. Ayla laughed and held the M card up high. "More letters, Grandma! More!"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Nathan held his lantern at the festival. Papa held his lantern too. It was dark outside. The lanterns were small paper balls with a light inside.

Nathan wanted his lantern to glow like the moon. But his lantern stayed dim. "Why is yours so bright?" he asked. "Let us walk up the hill," said Papa. "We will see."

They walked slowly. Nathan held his lantern with two hands. The grass by the path was wet. Nathan's shoes went squish, squish. Up they went, one step at a time.

At the top of the hill, Papa stopped. He turned the little stick on the lantern. Click. The lantern grew bright. "It was turned down," Papa said. "Now it is up."

Nathan looked at his own stick. He turned it. Click. His lantern glowed too. "Mine is like the moon!" he said. Down the hill, all the lanterns bobbed like little stars. Nathan walked with his, glowing all the way home.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Lea stood at the gate of the school playground. She held her mama's hand very tight. "I want a friend," she whispered. Mama smiled. "Let's look around."

A boy was pouring sand down a slide. The sand made a little pile at the bottom. Lea watched. He poured more sand. The pile grew high. Lea let go of mama's hand. She grabbed a small cup. She scooped her own sand. She poured it next to his pile. Now the pile was bigger.

"More sand, more pile," said the boy. He laughed. Lea laughed too. "I am Tom," he said. "I am Lea," she said. They made the pile big and round together. Mama sat on a bench close by. She waved. Lea waved back. Then she poured one more cup of sand.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
The bookmobile came to Luna's street. It was a little truck full of books. Luna held her mama's hand. "Can I take one home?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "First you get a card."

A kind man gave Luna a small card. It had her name on it. It felt like a gift in her hand. Luna picked a book about a red bird. The man stamped the back of it. The stamp made a mark. The mark told the day to bring the book back.

"I want to keep it forever," Luna said. She moved the book behind her back. The man shook his head, soft and kind. "Others need to read it too," he said. "Bring it back, and you can take a new one."

The shelf was empty where the bird book had been. Another girl was looking there. Luna saw her. She gave the book back to the man. "Can I take the moon one?" she asked. He smiled and stamped it.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Jasmine wanted to get the beanbag into the hoop. She threw it. It went low and fell on the grass. Her dog Max ran over and gave the beanbag a lick. "Yuck, Max," said Jasmine. She wiped it on her pants.

Dad rolled her a big red ball. Jasmine held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. She tried again. One hand, and the ball fell again. Then Dad said, "Try two hands." Jasmine made two arms like a big bowl. The ball went in. "I got it!" she said. Max wagged his furry tail.

Then Jasmine looked at the hoop. She held the beanbag up high. She threw it high. The beanbag went in. "One, two, three!" she counted, jumping. Max barked, and Jasmine hugged the ball with both hands.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Emile went to the vet with his dad. There was a small gray rabbit in a cage. Emile wanted to take him home. The vet opened the cage. She put the rabbit on the table. The rabbit's nose went up and down, up and down.

The vet gave Emile a soft brush. Emile brushed the rabbit's back. The rabbit pushed his head under Emile's hand. "He likes that," said the vet. Emile gave the rabbit a green leaf. The rabbit took it in his teeth. He chewed and chewed.

Dad put the rabbit in a box with holes. At home, Emile put water in a little bowl. The rabbit drank. Then he sat still and closed his eyes. Emile gave him one soft kiss on his head. "Good night, rabbit," said Emile. The rabbit's ears went down, slow and sleepy.

activity: making an art or craft project
story: Clara sat at the big art table. She was making a butterfly with paper and glue. She wanted it to look cute, with shiny wings. First she spread glue on the wings. Then she took the glitter jar. She sprinkled glitter all over the paper. She shook off the extra glitter. Where had the glitter gone? Some fell off onto the table. But the wings were still shiny. Clara looked closely. The glitter stayed only where the glue was. The dry parts were plain paper. Was it the glue that held it? She drew a fish on a new paper. She put glue only on its tail. She sprinkled glitter again. She tipped the paper sideways. The loose glitter slid off, like snow. The tail sparkled. "Look," said Clara. "Glue first, then sparkle." She held up her shiny fish.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Maeva wanted to show him her park. She put bread in her little bag. "We can feed the ducks," she said.

The park smelled like grass and flowers. Grandpa sat on a warm bench. Maeva stood by the pond. It was quiet. No ducks came. The ducks were far away on the other side. Maeva waited. Her arms felt tired of holding the bag.

Then she tore a piece of bread. She dropped a tiny bit in the water. Plip. One duck turned its head. Maeva dropped another bit. Plip. The duck swam fast. Then more ducks came. They came and came. "Grandpa, look!" Maeva yelled. "My bread brought them!"

Grandpa laughed and helped her tear more pieces. The ducks ate from the edge of the water. Then Maeva saw something small and fluffy. A line of ducklings paddled behind one big duck. "Babies!" said Maeva. She dropped one last soft piece. The littlest duckling grabbed it first.
